annotations.annotation_text: Page 312 opens Book 2, Chapter 3 ("The Tavern") during the Age of Heroes phase. This passage continues HCE behind the bar at his Chapelizod pub, the Norwegian Captain tale, the television broadcast, the twelve customers drinking and judging, featuring HCE, the Twelve Customers, Butt and Taff. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp
McHugh, Roland. Annotations to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/annotationstofin0000mchu_h5g8
Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com
JJDA: Finnegans Wake Genetic Edition. https://jjda.ie

annotations.annotation_text: The movable hump (312.06): the suit never fits because the Captain's hunchback keeps shifting with the swell of the sea waves. Symbolizes HCE's fluctuating moral guilt and bodily deformity.
sources: Hart, Clive. Structure and Motif in Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/structuremotifin0000hart

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 312 ("The Tavern"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Heroes dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: The mariner's departure (312.15): the Captain curses the tailor, refuses to pay for the ill-fitting suit, and sails back to sea, repeating the conflict across three seven-year cycles.
The Flying Dutchman myth (312.22): the Captain embodies the cursed mariner doomed to wander stormy seas until redeemed by the love and domestic sacrament of a faithful woman.
sources: Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Norse linguistic layer (312.30): Joyce saturates the text with Scandinavian loanwords (Danish, Norwegian, Swedish) reflecting the Norse maritime heritage of Dublin.
sources: Contemporary Literature Press: Scandinavian Languages in FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
